items.prompt: Why do living cells need a steady supply of oxygen?

options.label: To break down food and release the energy stored inside it
options.feedback: Inside every cell, oxygen combines with food to release the energy the cell needs to work, in a process much like a slow, controlled burn.

options.label: To keep the cell's outer wall from collapsing
options.feedback: A cell's outer wall is held together by its own structure, not propped up by a supply of oxygen.

options.label: To give cells their colour
options.feedback: The colour of a cell or tissue comes from other substances entirely; oxygen supply has nothing to do with it.

options.label: To cool the cell down after it has been working hard
options.feedback: Oxygen is a fuel for releasing energy, not a coolant; using it can actually generate warmth rather than remove it.

items.ok_line: Every cell runs a tiny, steady burn, and oxygen is what feeds it.
items.ko_line: Oxygen's job inside a cell has to do with releasing energy from food.
items.exp_title: A slow burn inside every cell
items.exp_text: Food carries stored energy that a cell cannot use until it is released. Combining that food with oxygen inside the cell releases the energy in a controlled way, much like a slow burn. Living cells need a steady supply of oxygen to break down food and release the energy stored inside it.

items.prompt: Ants and beetles have no lungs at all. How do they actually get the air they need?

options.label: Through their mouths, swallowed down into their stomachs
options.feedback: Swallowed air would only reach the digestive system, not the tissues throughout the body that need oxygen.

options.label: Through a network of tiny tubes running from small holes in the body straight to every cell
options.feedback: Small openings along an insect's body lead into a branching network of tubes that carries air directly to tissues throughout the body, with no lungs involved at all.

options.label: Through their skin absorbing air like a sponge
options.feedback: An insect's outer covering is a hard, largely sealed shell, not a soft absorbent surface for air to soak through.

options.label: They do not need air; their bodies run on stored water instead
options.feedback: Insects need a steady supply of air just as other animals do; they simply move it through the body differently.

items.ok_line: No lungs needed when tiny tubes reach every cell directly.
items.ko_line: An insect's body has small openings that lead somewhere very specific.
items.exp_text: Small openings dot an insect's body wall, each one leading into a branching network of tiny tubes. That network carries air directly through the body, reaching individual cells without any need for lungs or a bloodstream to carry the gas along the way. Ants and beetles get the air they need through a network of tiny tubes running from small holes in the body straight to every cell.

items.prompt: This tube network works well for a small insect. Why wouldn't the same system work for a much larger animal?

options.label: Because large animals do not actually need much oxygen
options.feedback: A larger body contains far more cells overall, so it generally needs more oxygen delivered, not less.

options.label: Because the tubes would be too heavy for a large body to carry
options.feedback: The tubes themselves are extremely light; weight is not what limits how far this kind of system can reach.

options.label: Because air moving passively along a tube only reaches a short distance before it runs out
options.feedback: Air drifting through a tube network relies on passive movement, which works over the short distances found within a small body but cannot reach far enough within a much larger one.

options.label: Because large animals have thicker skin that would block the tube openings
options.feedback: Skin thickness plays no role here; the limitation comes from how far air can travel passively along a tube, not from anything blocking an opening.

items.ok_line: Passive drifting only carries air so far before it simply stops moving.
items.ko_line: Think about how the air actually moves along those tubes, and how far that kind of movement can reach.
items.exp_title: A system with a limited reach
items.exp_text: Air inside this tube network is not actively pumped; it drifts passively along the tubes from the opening toward the cells that need it. items.prompt: A fish never breathes air the way a land animal does. How does it get the oxygen it needs?

options.label: It stores air in a pouch before diving underwater
options.feedback: A fish does not store a pouch of air before swimming; it draws oxygen continuously from the water around it.

options.label: It produces its own oxygen internally, without needing any from outside
options.feedback: No fish manufactures its own oxygen; like other animals, it depends on an outside source to supply what its cells need.

options.label: It absorbs oxygen from the air directly through its scales
options.feedback: Scales are not built to absorb gas; oxygen uptake happens at the gills, not through the scaled surface of the body.

options.label: Its gills draw dissolved oxygen already present in the water directly into its blood
options.feedback: A fish's gills are thin folds packed with blood vessels, built to pull the oxygen already dissolved in water straight into the bloodstream.

items.ok_line: No breath of air needed when the water itself already carries the gas.
items.ko_line: A fish's gills are built for one very specific job, involving the water flowing past them.
items.exp_text: Water itself carries a small amount of dissolved oxygen, enough to sustain life within it. A fish's gills are thin folds packed with blood vessels, positioned so that water flowing past them lets that dissolved oxygen pass directly into the blood. A fish gets the oxygen it needs because its gills draw dissolved oxygen already present in the water directly into its blood.

items.prompt: Plants take carbon dioxide straight from the air, yet most cannot take nitrogen from the air the same direct way. Why not?

options.label: Because the bond joining nitrogen's two atoms is too strong for a plant's own cells to break apart
options.feedback: Certain soil bacteria have the chemistry needed to split that strong bond and convert nitrogen into a form a plant's roots can absorb, a task ordinary plant cells cannot do alone.

options.label: Because there is far too little nitrogen in the air for a plant to notice
options.feedback: Nitrogen is actually the most plentiful gas in the air; scarcity is not the obstacle here.

options.label: Because a plant's roots are physically too large to absorb a gas
options.feedback: Roots readily absorb water and dissolved minerals from soil; size is not what stops them from taking in nitrogen gas.

options.label: Because plants only ever absorb gases through their flowers
options.feedback: Plants absorb gases mainly through their leaves, not through their flowers, and that is not the reason nitrogen poses a problem.

items.ok_title: A bond plant cells can't touch
items.ok_line: Some help from underground is needed to break what a plant's own cells cannot.
items.ko_line: Nitrogen is common enough in the air. The real obstacle is chemical.
items.exp_title: A bond only certain bacteria can break
items.exp_text: The two atoms in a nitrogen molecule are joined by an unusually strong bond, the same bond that keeps nitrogen gas from reacting easily with anything. items.prompt: Animals that live permanently high on a mountain often carry more oxygen-carrying red blood cells than their lowland relatives. Why?

options.label: Because the cold temperature at altitude directly produces extra blood cells
options.feedback: Cold alone does not directly cause a body to produce more blood cells; the real driver is the shortage of oxygen molecules in each breath at altitude.

options.label: Because thinner air up there delivers fewer oxygen molecules with each breath, so more blood cells are needed to gather enough
options.feedback: With fewer oxygen molecules arriving in every breath at altitude, a body compensates by carrying more of the cells that gather up and transport whatever oxygen is available.

options.label: Because mountain animals eat a different diet than lowland ones
options.feedback: Diet differences do not explain this particular change; the extra blood cells are a direct response to how much oxygen is available in each breath.

options.label: Because there is more sunlight at altitude, which stimulates blood cell growth
options.feedback: Sunlight exposure is not what drives this change; it comes from the body responding to how little oxygen each breath actually delivers.

items.ok_line: Fewer oxygen molecules per breath means the body carries more collectors for what is there.
items.ko_line: The real driver has to do with how few oxygen molecules arrive in each breath up there.
items.exp_title: More collectors for a thinner supply
items.exp_text: High on a mountain, each breath delivers fewer oxygen molecules than the same breath would at sea level. items.prompt: Why does your breathing speed up when you run, compared with when you are sitting still?

options.label: Because running makes the lungs physically shrink, forcing quicker breaths
options.feedback: The lungs do not shrink during exercise; breathing speeds up to deliver more oxygen, not because there is suddenly less room inside them.

options.label: Because moving the legs somehow pumps extra air into the lungs directly
options.feedback: Leg movement does not pump air into the lungs; breathing itself speeds up because working cells need oxygen delivered faster.

options.label: Because running cells burn more fuel for energy and need oxygen delivered faster to keep up
options.feedback: Working muscles burn through fuel much faster than resting ones, and faster breathing brings in oxygen quickly enough to match that faster demand.

options.label: Because running raises body temperature, and hot lungs need less air
options.feedback: A rise in body temperature does not reduce the air a person needs; if anything, working muscles need more oxygen delivered, not less.

items.ok_line: Faster burning means the body has to bring in oxygen faster too.
items.ko_line: Faster breathing during exercise is about keeping up with how quickly cells are burning fuel.
items.exp_text: Running muscles burn through fuel far faster than muscles at rest, and that faster burning needs oxygen delivered at a matching pace. Breathing speeds up so that more oxygen reaches the blood in the same span of time. Breathing speeds up when you run because running cells burn more fuel for energy and need oxygen delivered faster to keep up.

items.prompt: You can hold your breath for a while, but eventually you have to breathe again. What actually triggers that urgent need?

options.label: The lungs running completely empty of air
options.feedback: The lungs still hold a good deal of air by the time the urge to breathe strikes; complete emptiness is not what triggers it.

options.label: A sudden drop in body temperature
options.feedback: Body temperature does not drop noticeably during a held breath; temperature is not the trigger involved here.

options.label: The muscles in the chest simply growing tired
options.feedback: Chest muscles do not tire out within the short span of a held breath; the urgent signal comes from something building up in the blood instead.

options.label: A buildup of carbon dioxide in the blood, rather than a lack of oxygen itself
options.feedback: While a breath is held, carbon dioxide steadily builds up in the blood, and it is that buildup, rather than a shortage of oxygen, that triggers the urgent signal to breathe again.

items.ok_title: It's the buildup, not the shortage
items.ok_line: What forces the next breath is what's piling up in the blood, not what's running out.
items.ko_line: The urge to breathe again comes from something accumulating in the blood while the breath is held.
items.exp_title: A signal from what's building up
items.exp_text: While a breath is held, oxygen is used up only slowly, but carbon dioxide keeps being produced and has nowhere to go. That rising level of carbon dioxide in the blood is what triggers the urgent, unmistakable need to breathe again. The urgent need to breathe is triggered by a buildup of carbon dioxide in the blood, rather than a lack of oxygen itself.

items.prompt: One kind of living thing breathes out a gas as waste, and another kind of living thing needs that very same gas to build its food. What does this describe?

options.label: A rare coincidence that happens only occasionally
options.feedback: This exchange is not occasional or rare; it happens constantly between countless living things sharing the same air.

options.label: An ongoing exchange of gases between different kinds of living things through the air
options.feedback: Animals release carbon dioxide as waste while breathing, and plants take in that same gas to build their food, releasing oxygen in turn for animals to breathe.

options.label: A one-way process where only plants ever benefit
options.feedback: The exchange runs in both directions: plants use what animals release, and animals in turn use what plants release.

options.label: A process that only happens during a single season each year
options.feedback: This exchange of gases continues constantly through every season, not only at one particular time of year.

items.ok_title: Waste for one, food for the other
items.ok_line: What one living thing breathes out is exactly what another is waiting to take in.
items.ko_line: This is neither rare nor one-way; think about what flows between different kinds of living things, and in which directions.
items.exp_text: Animals release carbon dioxide as waste with every breath, while plants take in that same gas to build their food. Plants, in turn, release oxygen as they do, and animals take that in to breathe. This describes an ongoing exchange of gases between different kinds of living things through the air.

items.prompt: Countless living things constantly use and release gases into the air. Why doesn't this throw the overall mix of gases permanently out of balance?

options.label: Because living things stop using gases once a certain balance is reached
options.feedback: Living things do not pause their breathing or feeding once a balance is reached; the balance is maintained while both processes keep running continuously.

options.label: Because the air holds an unlimited supply of every gas regardless of use
options.feedback: The air's supply of any single gas is not unlimited; the balance instead comes from how much is produced roughly matching how much is used.

options.label: Because the amount of oxygen produced by living things roughly matches the amount consumed by breathing and decay worldwide
options.feedback: Across the whole world, the oxygen released by countless living things roughly matches what is consumed by breathing and decay, keeping the balance steady over time.

options.label: Because only a small number of living things actually use any gas at all
options.feedback: An enormous number of living things use gases from the air constantly; it is the rough balance between production and use that keeps the mixture steady, not a small number of users.

items.ok_line: What's released roughly matches what's consumed, worldwide, all the time.
items.ko_line: Nothing about the air's supply is unlimited, and nothing about living things ever truly pauses. The balance comes from somewhere else.
items.exp_title: A rough balance, kept by countless living things
items.exp_text: Across the whole world, countless living things are constantly releasing gases into the air while countless others are constantly consuming them. The overall mix stays steady because the amount of oxygen produced by living things roughly matches the amount consumed by breathing and decay worldwide.
